anchor: I was angry with my friend
title: Title and composition
short: In Blake's Notebook the poem was first titled 'Christian Forbearance'; it was engraved in Songs of Experience (1794) as 'A Poison Tree'.
body: The Notebook draft's title makes the satire clear: what passes for Christian forbearance, refraining from expressing anger, is shown to breed hidden malice. The change to 'A Poison Tree' shifts the emphasis from the moral pretension to its fruit. The poem appeared in Songs of Experience (1794). Its brevity and nursery-rhyme manner disguise a psychological insight that later critics have compared to modern ideas of repression, though the language is that of Blake's own moral vision.

title: Telling wrath
short: Anger spoken to a friend ends; anger hidden from a foe grows. Compare 'let not the sun go down upon your wrath' (Ephesians 4:26).
body: The first stanza is a perfect antithesis: friend and foe, told and told not, end and grow. Ephesians 4:26 advises 'Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath'. Blake's paradox is that the conventional Christian virtue of suppressing anger towards an enemy (Matthew 5:44, 'Love your enemies') can produce the opposite of love. The Proverbs of Hell in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell make the same point: 'He who desires but acts not, breeds pestilence'.

anchor: And I watered it in fears
title: Metre and growth
short: Trochaic tetrameter couplets, mostly seven syllables, in the plain manner of a nursery rhyme or hymn.
body: Most lines have seven syllables and four stresses, beginning and ending on a stress (catalectic trochaic tetrameter), with an initial unstressed 'And' added in several lines. The rhyming couplets and simple vocabulary resemble children's verse and Isaac Watts's Divine Songs, which Blake often parodied. The metaphor of the wrath as a plant is introduced without comment: 'it' is watered by fearful tears, so that the image grows as the anger does.

title: Smiles and wiles
short: The anger is nourished by false smiles and deceits, as a plant is by sunlight: hypocrisy feeds the hidden hatred.
body: Tears water the plant and smiles 'sun' it, so that both grief and pretended friendliness feed the growth. 'Wiles' are tricks or stratagems. The speaker's hypocrisy is described with the gardener's care, a chilling domestic image. Blake's 'The Human Abstract', in the same volume, also shows a tree of cruelty, Mystery, rooted in false virtues and watered with 'holy fears'.

title: The apple
short: The fruit of the tree recalls the forbidden fruit of Eden (Genesis 3), traditionally pictured as an apple.
body: Genesis does not name the fruit, but the apple was its traditional representation. In Blake's poem the tree is not God's but the speaker's, and the fruit is a lure: the foe is tempted to steal it, as Eve was tempted. The speaker thus plays the role of the tempter, or of the jealous God who forbids. 'Bright' stresses its allure. The tree also anticipates the Tree of Mystery in The Book of Ahania and The Four Zoas.

anchor: he knew that it was mine
title: he knew that it was mine
short: The foe covets the apple because it belongs to the speaker; envy draws him as the speaker intended.
body: The line is ambiguous: the foe may want the apple because he knows it is the speaker's, out of envy or rivalry, or he may recognise it as the product of the speaker's hatred. Critics have noted that the poem implicates both men: the speaker cultivates a trap, and the foe is a thief. The dash at the end of the line in this text (as in many printings) creates a pause before the night theft.

title: stole into my garden
short: The foe steals into the garden at night, a thief entering Eden; 'stole' means both crept and committed theft.
body: The verb 'stole' means crept stealthily, and the context of the apple adds the sense of theft. The garden is the speaker's private Eden, and the trespass recalls Satan's entry into Paradise in Paradise Lost (Book IV), where Satan leaps the wall like a thief. The speaker's garden of hatred contrasts with 'The Garden of Love' in the same volume.

title: the pole
short: The pole is the sky or the pole star; night has hidden the heavens, so the theft is unseen.
body: In poetic usage 'the pole' could mean the sky, the heavens, or the pole star (Latin polus, the sky; Greek polos, the axis). 'When the night had veiled the pole' means when darkness had covered the sky. The elevated phrase contrasts with the poem's simple diction, giving a touch of Miltonic gloom to the murder. The night also conceals the speaker's own guilt: he cultivates the tree in daylight with smiles, but the deed is done in darkness. 'Veiled' suggests concealment and mystery, a word Blake elsewhere associates with the veil of the Temple and of priestly secrecy.

anchor: In the morning, glad, I see
title: The present tense and gladness
short: The tense shifts to the present, and the speaker is 'glad' to see his foe dead under the tree.
body: The narrative has been in the past tense; the final couplet moves into the present, as if the scene were before us. The word 'glad', isolated between commas, is the poem's most disturbing word: it shows the speaker's satisfaction. 'Outstretched' could mean dead or poisoned, or merely lying under the tree; most readers take him to be dead. The poem ends without moral comment, leaving the reader to judge the 'Christian forbearance' that has produced this result.
